title: Big Trouble in Little China: The Game: The Review
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XVwO4OvjwI4

Daniel (@dungeondive) has now played Everything Epic's Big Trouble in Little China four times, and he opens his review with two verdicts. First, it's a "once-a-year game": not a weakness, just the kind of special-occasion box you bring out annually, enjoy, forget the details of, and rediscover. Second, two-thirds of it is great and one-third falls flat.

The great part is Act One. Each hero pursues main quests through a short-passage quest book (he sees the seeds of Secrets of the Lost Station here, done better because the book is lighter and the board decisions matter more), alongside three stacks of side quests, all against a good timer and a bad timer that shape the finale. The dice system has you slot body, mind and spirit dice into action rows, with glowing slots giving "epic" versions. Then there's the fate track, a shared pool of dice that lets you tempt fate for bigger actions at the risk of outright death. He loves it as rare, proper push-your-luck.

Act Two, the showdown with Lo Pan and the Three Storms, is where it stumbles: ambiguous quest cards, board misprints, and setup that sends you to BGG every time. Enemy variety is thin too, and with the licence likely gone there will be no expansion. He hasn't yet tried the Kickstarter's Legacy of Lo Pan campaign. Still, it captures the film's whimsical weirdness. Recommended, with a warning about that second act.

----

Do you have "once-a-year games" on your shelf, ones you love but deliberately ration? What earns a game that status for you?
